lesson.title: au & du Fusions
lesson.subtitle: à + le = au, de + le = du, de + les = des: mandatory contractions as word-glue.

hook.title: Why à + le and de + le Fuse on Impact
hook.content: Masculine consonant nouns fuse mandatorily with à and de: à + le = au (/o/), de + le = du (/dy/), and plural à + les = aux, de + les = des. Meanwhile, feminine consonant nouns stay separate (à la gare, de la gare) and vowel/mute-H nouns elide (à l'hôtel, de l'hôtel)!

footnotes.title: The 3-way check: Vowel (à l'/de l'), Feminine (à la/de la), Masculine (au/du)
footnotes.content: Check the first letter and gender of the noun before choosing the preposition form.

pattern.title: Mandatory Fusions: au / du vs. à la / de la vs. à l' / de l'
pattern.content: Apply the 3-way check across places in town.
pattern.linguist_note: Enclitic fusion of preposition + masculine/plural definite article is mandatory in French.
pattern.trap_note: Never write *à le cinéma or *de le restaurant — always fuse into au cinéma and du restaurant!

exercises.prompt: Match each destination or origin with its correct French preposition + article:
exercises.target_answer: au cinéma, du train, à la gare, de la maison, à l'hôtel
exercises.meaning: to the cinema (le cinéma, m.), from the train (le train, m.), to the station (la gare, f.), from the house (la maison, f.), to the hotel (l'hôtel, mute H)
exercises.explanation: Masculine consonant fuses (au/du); feminine stays separate (à la/de la); vowel/mute-H elides (à l'/de l').

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'I am coming from the restaurant and going to the station' (le restaurant, la gare):
options: Je viens de le restaurant et je vais à la gare
Je viens du restaurant et je vais au gare
Je viens du restaurant et je vais à la gare
exercises.target_answer: Je viens du restaurant et je vais à la gare
exercises.meaning: from the restaurant (du) and to the station (à la)
exercises.explanation: de + le restaurant fuses into du restaurant; feminine la gare takes à la gare.

exercises.prompt: Fuse the preposition and article: 'to the restaurant' (à + le restaurant) →
Reply to the question in French:
exercises.spoken_question: Où est-ce que vous habitez maintenant ?
exercises.reply_idea: Reply that we live in Paris now.
cues: Place à Paris maintenant after the verb.
exercises.explanation: To answer an où question with a city, French pairs habiter with the preposition à: Nous habitons à Paris.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Nous allons au restaurant à côté de la gare
exercises.target_answer: Nous allons au restaurant à côté de la gare
exercises.meaning: We are going to the restaurant next to the station
exercises.explanation: au restaurant (m. fusion) + de la gare (f. non-fusion).
exercises.affirmation: You contrasted au restaurant and de la gare accurately.

summary.outcome: Apply the 3-way check (au/du vs. à la/de la vs. à l'/de l') across masculine, feminine, and vowel-initial nouns.

use_example.german: Je sors de l'hôtel et je vais au café en face de la gare.
use_example.english: I leave the hotel and go to the café across from the station.

summary.takeaway: Vowel → à l' / de l'; Feminine → à la / de la; Masculine → au / du.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1302] Chez, the House Word): see how au & du Fusions leads directly into Chez, the House Word.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "We are going to the restaurant next to the station" in French:
twist.target_answer: Nous allons au restaurant à côté de la gare
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Nous allons au restaurant à côté de la gare" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of au & du Fusions.

à.etymology_derivation: Latin ad 'to' — English kept it in adhere, advance, admire. With le it fuses: à + le = au.

de.etymology_derivation: Latin dē 'down from' — of and from in one small word.

au.etymology_derivation: Never *à le: French fuses them into au (/o/). Plural à + les = aux.

du.etymology_derivation: Does double duty: 'from the' (du train) and the masculine partitive 'some' (du pain, du café).

des.etymology_derivation: Plural of un/une: where English says bare 'books', French says des livres ('some books').

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

restaurant.etymology_derivation: From restaurer 'to restore' — originally a restoring broth sold in Paris in 1765.

gare.etymology_derivation: Originally a river shelter where boats pulled in.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

cinéma.context_phrase: On va au cinéma ce soir ?
cinéma.context_translation: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?
cinéma.etymology_derivation: Invented by the Lumière brothers in Lyon in 1895.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
